narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated a 60% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt—meaning failure was judged more likely than not. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty: the same assessment implies a 40% chance of passing. The strongest factor driving the denial was your undergraduate GPA of 2.50, which is below the 3.23 average among accepted students; this pushed the prediction toward failure. The second most influential factor was your third-year class decile of 6.00. Because this is slightly above the accepted-student average of 5.79, it worked in your favor and pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the GPA concern. The third factor, your middle family-income bracket, added a smaller push toward failure; middle income is common among accepted students, at 34.8%, so this was a modest factor rather than a decisive one. To improve a future application, focus on demonstrable academic strength: take additional rigorous coursework, consider a post-baccalaureate or master’s program, aim for a stronger LSAT if you retake it, and seek admissions advising. Ask schools for feedback and consider applying where your record and improvement can be reviewed holistically.
